title: Not Your Keys, Not Your DAT
sourceSections: People are worried about non-GAAP accounting

illustration.alt: Nathaniel Bradley watches an empty withdrawal hatch at Biconomy while a ledger shows 1,309 Bitcoin credited to Datavault AI and Scilex holds newly issued shares.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Datavault issued 278.9 million shares to Scilex in exchange for about 1,309 Bitcoin credited through off-chain entries at Biconomy. Because Datavault could not withdraw the remaining balance onto the Bitcoin blockchain, its accountants determined that the credits did not qualify as company-owned digital assets.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: During the digital-asset-treasury boom, the market seemed willing to pay $2 of stock value for $1 of Bitcoin; in Datavault’s case, it ultimately appeared to have paid $2 for $0 of withdrawable Bitcoin.

preschool.title: The Bitcoin That Wouldn’t Come Out
preschool.lesson: A balance shown on a crypto exchange’s private ledger may not qualify as a company-owned digital asset if the company cannot withdraw the Bitcoin onto the blockchain.
paragraphs:
In 2025, Wall Street loved a strange new trick:
Buy Bitcoin, watch your company’s value rise up quick.
A hundred million dollars in coins might make twice that appear;
Everyone knew it couldn’t last, so deals came fast that year.

Datavault AI was worth about $35 million one day,
with 116.7 million shares near thirty cents in play.
It sold Scilex 278.9 million shares in a trade,
at $0.5378 each—and Bitcoin was how Scilex paid.

About 1,309 Bitcoin, then worth near $150 million, appeared
in Datavault’s Biconomy account, and shareholders cheered.
CEO Nathaniel Bradley praised biotech, blockchain, and AI;
the stock hit $3.118—a $973 million high.

But these were off-chain credits: Biconomy’s private record showed the sum,
not Bitcoin on the public blockchain where coins can go and come.
Datavault sold 491 back to Scilex for $40.5 million in cash,
then tried withdrawing the rest—and ran into a crash.

The withdrawal would not complete; no on-chain coins came through.
Accountants said the old financial statements were no longer true.
The Bitcoin did not qualify as Datavault’s asset after all,
and its stock closed down 50% after the news’s fall.

The market once paid $2 in stock for $1 of Bitcoin in sight.
Now it seemed to have paid $2 for $0. Oops—not quite right!

What happened? Scilex credited about 1,309 Bitcoin to Datavault AI on Biconomy’s private, off-chain ledger, but Datavault could not withdraw the remaining coins to an external blockchain wallet. Its accountants concluded that the Bitcoin had never qualified as Datavault’s digital asset.

stories.sourceSection: People are worried about non-GAAP accounting

illustration.alt: Jonathan Weil points to Anthropic’s rising stock-like contracts, which show a GAAP loss for Anthropic and paper gains for Amazon and Alphabet.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Convertible notes, preferred stock, and purchase agreements were partly classified as derivative liabilities and marked to market, so Anthropic’s rising valuation created a non-cash accounting loss for Anthropic and paper gains for investors.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Anthropic’s value soared—a good thing—but its unusual stock-like contracts made that success appear as an approximately $80 billion GAAP loss.

preschool.title: The Good News That Looked Like a Loss
preschool.lesson: Because Anthropic’s unusual stock-like contracts were classified as mark-to-market derivative liabilities, its rising value created a huge non-cash GAAP loss, even though ordinary issued stock would not.
paragraphs:
As Anthropic PBC prepared for an IPO day,
its first-half numbers made eyebrows sway.
GAAP showed an $80.7 billion loss in red,
while adjusted net income was $2.7 billion ahead.

Anthropic had sold Google and Amazon unusual deals:
convertible notes, preferred stock, and agreements with seals.
They worked much like shares, but GAAP gave them a name—
“derivative liabilities,” repriced whenever values changed.

Anthropic’s value rose by about $80 billion—good news!
The investors gained on paper from the stock they could use.
But “mark to market” measured those contracts anew,
so Anthropic booked a matching paper loss coming through.

No mountain of cash had gone rolling away;
it was an accounting result of the higher price that day.
About $72 billion in liability losses left adjusted profit’s sight,
and once the deals become ordinary stock, that repricing will stop outright.

Jonathan Weil noted an odd double view:
Amazon and Alphabet counted their paper gains as earnings coming through.
If Anthropic removes the corresponding loss from its adjusted display,
should analysts remove the investors’ gains in the very same way?

Warren Buffett had warned of distortion before,
when 2016 rules counted rising stocks that Berkshire Hathaway bore.
Still, an owner’s gain need not be an issuing company’s loss:
stock can create value—it needn’t leave someone else paying the cost.

What happened? Anthropic’s stock-like financing contracts rose in value and were treated under US GAAP as mark-to-market liabilities, producing an $80.7 billion first-half net loss that was mostly non-cash. Analysts excluded much of that loss to calculate $2.7 billion of adjusted net income, while Amazon and Alphabet included related paper gains in their own earnings measures.

illustration.alt: Xavier De Pauw at Monument Bank offers a portfolio-backed loan while an ordinary investor’s unsold shares remain secured as collateral.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: An investor pledges appreciated securities as collateral and borrows against them rather than selling. The loan proceeds are not taxable income, and after the investor’s death, the heirs’ stepped-up basis can eliminate capital-gains tax on the earlier appreciation before they sell shares to repay the debt.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: A tax-and-borrowing strategy associated with billionaires is being standardized for ordinary investors, who can now be invited to “adopt a billionaire mindset.”

preschool.title: Borrow Like a Billionaire
preschool.lesson: “Buy, borrow, die” means borrowing against appreciated shares instead of selling them, then using the stepped-up tax basis at death so heirs can repay the loan without tax on the earlier gains.
paragraphs:
Suppose a stock portfolio, worth $100 million,
held gains that had quietly grown by the million.
Sell shares for more than their purchase-day price,
and capital-gains tax may claim its own slice.

Instead, pledge those shares as collateral—a tie
that secures a bank loan while the stock stays nearby.
Borrow $50 million at six percent due;
a loan isn't income, so no gains tax comes through.

The interest is $3 million year after year;
with eight-percent growth, $8 million may appear.
The interest can simply be added to debt—
if markets keep rising as averages suggest.

When the owner dies, the heirs’ tax basis resets
to the shares’ current value, with earlier gains swept.
They sell enough stock to repay what was owed;
the rest can stay theirs after settling the load.

Deloitte estimates such lending at $5.4 trillion,
against stocks, bonds, funds, and crypto by the billion.
Deloitte’s Eric Gutzwiller said it once served the rich;
now affluent and retail customers are making the switch.

At Monument Bank, Xavier De Pauw planned to lend
to investors with a few hundred thousand to spend.
They could “adopt a billionaire mindset,” he said—
a billionaire tax strategy, now widely spread.

What happened? Banks and brokerages increasingly lend people money secured by their investment portfolios, letting them spend without selling appreciated shares. If the borrower dies holding the shares, heirs receive a stepped-up tax basis and can sell enough to repay the loan without owing capital-gains tax on the pre-death increase.

illustration.alt: Tarek Mansour presents a nationwide Kalshi sports-contract market while Utah officials block it with the Utah Constitution and state gambling law.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: Customers trade sports-event contracts with one another on Kalshi’s federally regulated prediction exchange; Kalshi argues that federal commodities regulation preempts state gambling rules, while states argue the contracts are sports bets governed or banned by state law.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Kalshi’s position implies a newly discovered federal constitutional priority: overriding century-old state gambling laws so eighteen-year-olds can have a liquid nationwide market for sports bets.

preschool.title: Kalshi, Utah, and the Fifty Rulebooks
preschool.lesson: Kalshi offers peer-to-peer sports-event contracts under federal commodities regulation, but states including Utah argue that those contracts are gambling subject to state bans and gaming laws.
paragraphs:
Tarek Mansour of Kalshi said, “Our market’s not the same:
No sportsbook house takes the other side of every game.”
On Kalshi, traders meet as peers—one “yes,” one “no”;
Their prices join a nationwide pool, then final scores will show.

A bar can bet against its team to hedge its beer-sales risk:
If cheering crowds don’t come, the contract softens business’s dip.
Mansour said sportsbooks aren’t used that way—but there’s a hitch:
Mattress Mack has hedged there for years, so that claim needs a switch.

Mansour wanted federal rules, not fifty state commands;
He pictured New York Stock Exchange rules changing across the lands.
A national pool, he argued, keeps trading deep and wide,
While state-by-state restrictions split the traders up by side.

But Utah sued Kalshi, saying gambling isn’t welcome there;
Its constitution has banned it for 130 years with care.
And in 2018, the Supreme Court said each state may choose
The sports-betting rules it wants to keep, permit, or refuse.

So Kalshi and the CFTC arrived at something new:
Old state bans might yield to federal commodities law’s view.
The strange result: a vital federal interest, it would seem,
Is liquid nationwide sports-event trading for an eighteen-year-old’s team.

What happened? Kalshi treated sports wagers as federally regulated peer-to-peer event contracts, while Utah and other states sued under their own gambling laws. The dispute asks whether federal commodities law overrides state sports-gambling rules, despite the Supreme Court’s 2018 recognition of state authority.

And in 2018, the Supreme Court said each state may choose
The sports-betting rules it wants to keep, permit, or refuse.

So Kalshi and the CFTC arrived at something new:
Old state bans might yield to federal commodities law’s view.
The strange result: a vital federal interest, it would seem,
Is liquid nationwide sports-event trading for an eighteen-year-old’s team.

What happened? Kalshi treated sports wagers as federally regulated peer-to-peer event contracts, while Utah and other states sued under their own gambling laws. The dispute asks whether federal commodities law overrides state sports-gambling rules, despite the Supreme Court’s 2018 recognition of state authority.
